reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: This is a fascinating and well-written paper. It provides a much-needed analysis of the phylogenetic pattern of pollen morphology and produces insights into the timing of angiosperm diversification. My expertise is in palynology and less so in phylogenetic methods, so my comments focus more on the morphological analysis than the phylogenetic work. That said, however, my main concern with the paper is the angiosperm phylogeny used in the study. The authors produce their own from published sequence data instead of relying on recently published phylogenies (e.g., Zuntini et al 2024). I do not believe that this will affect the interpretations or conclusions of the paper, given the broad patterns that this paper focuses on, but the authors should be aware that there will be a mismatch between the superorder clades that they discuss (Fabids, Malvids, Superasterids, Superrosids) and more recent delimitations. Given the speed at which genomic data is now being accumulated, and the potential for future reorganization of the angiosperm phylogeny, it would be helpful if the authors included a spreadsheet of the genera and orders they include within their larger named groups to help with transparency and interpretability of their analysis. I would also strongly encourage the authors to publish the list of genera in their analysis and their character scores as a second spreadsheet. This again would improve the transparency and interpretability of their analysis and encourage others to build on their work. Section-by-section points below: Abstract • “Endowed” is an odd word choice. Maybe simply “composed”? Introduction • Page 3, line 3: “synapomorphy OF equatorially tricolpate pollen” • “the processes of angiosperm pollen diversification”: This paper is more about pattern than process. Suggest that you emphasize the importance of documenting pattern to infer process. • “This gap hinders, and may even distort, our understanding of angiosperm radiation, particularly regarding deep evolutionary processes”: I agree with the sentiment, but it would be better if the authors made a more explicit statement of how this is a result of the previous sentence. Results • p 4: “a discrete-coded matrix”: Should note that 20 characters were coded, and the larger groupings (aperture, exine, shape) should be introduced and described/defined. Otherwise, the meaning of the shorthand terms used in the results (aperture, exine, shape) are hard to understand. • p 4: “The topology is congruent with recent phylogenetic frameworks 48-50”: Note that Zuntini et al 2024 does NOT have the same topology as previous phylogenies (e.g., APG IV) • p 5, paragraph 1: “plastome-based PPA tree”: Should include “the” before the word “plastome”. Also need to define what this is, particularly the acronym PPA. • p 5, paragraph 1: “a temporal pattern irreconcilable with current paleobotanical evidence”: It is not clear whether you are saying your results are irreconcilable or whether old tree scenarios are. Based on Coiro et al 2019 review of the Triassic fossil evidence, I would say that phylogenies that place the ancestral angiosperm node very early (Triassic or before) conflict most with the paleo record. • p 5, paragraph 2: “In our ordination analysis, we opted for Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS) to process the pollen data”: process is not the correct word. Interpret? Analyze? • p 5: Pollen morphospace occupation (and elsewhere): all palynological terms should be defined when first introduced. When mentioning a trait (e.g., polarity), mention which larger grouping it belongs to (aperture, exine, shape). • p 5, last paragraph: “Compared to the theoretical morphospace, the empirical morphospace occupies approximately 43% of the area on the left side”: Language here is too casual and imprecise. Right vs left is arbitrary in a multivariate analysis. What is important is that only a portion of the theoretical morphospace is occupied. Instead of left and right, describe the axis by the traits with which it most strongly covaries, positively and negatively. • p 6, paragraph 1: “the highest levels”: What does this mean? • p 6, paragraph 1: “overall pollen disparity”: Is this within-clade or between clades? • p 7, paragraph 1: “overlap between the two lists”: What two lists? If this is a reference to Table S5, include the reference and explain the difference between the two sets of rankings. Discussion • p 9, paragraph 2: “These differences emphasize that varying scales and subjects of observation can yield different evolutionary insights.”: Is the argument that early pollen evolution was constrained? The wording is a little vague. • p 9, paragraph 3: “In animal taxa, basally-branching groups often exhibit higher levels of disparity than their more derived counterparts 15,24,25, a pattern also observed in the morphospace of angiosperm flowers 41,56.” This is repetitive, as the same point is made in the previous paragraph. • p 10: Synchronous Evolution of Pollen and Leaves: This section is speculative and has a tenuous connection to the rest of the paper. How does tricolpate pollen relate to hot wet environments? Recommend removing this section. • p 11, last paragraph: “while the Malpighiales are associated with the development of neotropical rainforests”: Need a citation for this. Malpighiales is a large and diverse order, but it is Malvales that is the more important Neotropical clade. Conclusions • Appreciate the mention of extinct diversity! Methods • p 15, paragraph 3: “with further subdivisions for detailed analysis”: As noted at the start of the review, you should specify that you are following APG IV clade deliminations, not Zuntini et al 2024. It is important that you list the orders and genera within each larger named group in a supplemental spreadsheet. • p 16, paragraph 1: More detail on how the theoretical morphospace was calculated would be helpful. Presumably these are random permutations of the pollen characters in Table S2 (which should be referenced here). Supporting information • Supplementary Table 2: A third column is needed to indicate which larger grouping each trait falls under (aperture, shape, exine). Happy to clarify any of the above comments. Surangi Punyasena (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: Dear Authors and Editor, I have reviewed the paper entitled "Pulsed evolution shaped angiosperm pollen disparity". I think it is a good study addressing the evolution of a very important plant character. On the one hand the authors scored several pollen traits to characterize pollen grains across a large set of species. On the author hand the authors generated a time calibrated molecular phylogeny of plants to look at the evolutionary history of these characters. By combining these two datasets and using comparative methods, they make a case for pulsed evolution of pollen. I think the paper is clearly written and the authors build on their work on this topic, namely the extensive series of papers on the “Evolution of Angiosperm Pollen”. A few questions I have are the following: Why a genus level pollen dataset? Are all the genera included monophyletic? Do the authors have any concern that if a genus in the dataset is not monophyletic their results would change? What happens when a genus is polymorphic for a trait? How does it get scored? What effect does it have to calculate disparity through time when the terminals in the tree are genera and not species? When assigning shapes to the pollen, one character involves "Basic shape" whereas a second "Outline in polar view". It is not clear to me how these are independant. Also, the character states of the second one includes as state 0 "circular & elliptic". Where would an elliptic pollen grain in polar view fall in the "Basic shape" variable? Looking at studies that review these characteristics of pollen, Walker and Doyle (1975) for example divide pollen shape into two basic types: globose and boat shaped. Does this equal globose-like vs filiform? Hesse et al. (2009) divide shape into oblate, spheroidal and prolate. So perhaps a little explanation of how some of those variables were established would be useful. Why were the traditional shape scoreing not used? Several old and recent studies have used morphometrics, from traditional approaches employing length to width rations, to geometric morphometric techniques such as elliptic Fourier analyses. Is there a reason why the authors chose not to use a quantitative approach to measure pollen grain shape and instead stuck to a discrete and simplified way of scoring pollen? The size variable has very unequal bin sizes. How were those size classes determined? Maybe I missed it but the pollen characters used are subdivided into three subtypes but I don't think it is clear which characters are assigned to each subgroup. Maybe in Supplementary table 2 the subgroups could be pointed out. Supplemental Information Page 1, paragraph 2: change "Phylogenetic comparison methods" to "Phylogenetic comparative methods" I appreciate that all the scripts, data and code are made available.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: This study applies an impressive morphological dataset of pollen characters and a time-calibrated phylogeny to document morphospace occupation and changes in morphological diversity through time and across major angiosperm groups. I found this paper well-written and interesting to read. There are several points that I would like to highlight: 1) the taxon sampling for extant species is exceptionally good and the overall amount of missing data is low, an outcome that clearly reflects considerable effort by the authors; 2) I have no specific criticisms regarding the methods, as the authors employed and compared different ordination methods (NMDS and PCoA) as well as various and disparity indices (SOR, SOV, MPD, MDC). In my opinion, this is an interesting paper as allow us comparative analysis of morphological variation in other angiosperms organs, such as flowers, leaves, and wood providing a more comprehensive understanding of the evolutionary radiation of angiosperms. Major comment The lack of fossil data. Luo et al. are clearly aware of the limitation of this study is that the estimation of pollen variation through time is based solely on extant taxa. I find no adequate justification for completely disregarding the valuable knowledge that has been compiled over decades by the paleobotanical community on the fossil pollen record. In my view, the fossil pollen record represents the only direct source of information for assessing morphological disparity in the deep past, and its analysis and quantification are essential for a comprehensive understanding of evolutionary patterns over time. More reliable macroevolutionary inferences require the inclusion of fossil taxa, as there are many examples in which the fossil record contain much more information about past evolutionary patterns than phylogenies, for example preserving unique character combinations that have not seen in living species and consequently cannot be reconstructed in ancestral state reconstructions. Incorporating such fossil data could significantly change the observed patterns of disparity through time. The authors indicate that earlier studies fossil pollen (e.g., Lupia, 1999; Doyle 1977) “were constrained by a limited understanding of evolutionary relationships among groups and were restricted in geographical and temporal extent”. I agree with this assessment; however, I believe that significant progress has been made in recent decades to improve our understanding of the fossil pollen record. For example, new species have been described (many with a great detail) and new localities have been sampled greatly expanding the temporal and geographical coverage of available data. I am not saying that the fossil record is perfect, fossil data are subject to several biases, but also inferring these patterns using the phylogenies of extant taxa is not accurate. This is my main concern; the approach considered in this study, while methodologically sound with its scope, may fall short of what is expected for a Nature Communications paper, especially compared to a recent article on a similar topic (Clark et al. 2023 Nat Plants), which integrated fossil and extant data to assess morphological disparity. One potential solution for this pitfall is that the authors should be explicit about the estimations based only on extant taxa, for example in the title or in the abstract. I think that a section comparing the fossil record (not only the patterns observed by Lupia or Doyle) with your results is missing. For instance, based on your findings, you indicate that rates of pollen evolution remained stable during the mid-Cretaceous and Paleogene. However, what does the pollen fossil record reveal about the Late Cretaceous? How did morphological diversification proceed during this interval? Was it similarly stable and low, or were there notable shifts in morphology? Additionally, which new morphological characters first appeared during this period? A discussion of these aspects would significantly enrich the interpretation of your results within a broader evolutionary and paleobotanical context. The main strength of this paper, in my view, is that the authors, given their taxon sampling, are able to offer a comprehensive comparison of disparity variation among extant angiosperm clades or lineages and provide a further discussion on this variation. For example: -why some extant clades appeared more restricted in the space than others? I see that the authors explained this topic in the section of “extant angiosperm pollen morphospace”, however, it would be interesting to know, for example: -the extensive morphospace occupation by fabids aligns with patterns observed in studies of floral or leaf morphospaces? -Why do monocots exhibit the highest morphological disparity despite not occupying the largest areas of the morphospace? -The ANA grade, Chloranthales, and the other superasterids groups have the lowest contributions to the overall disparity, however, to my knowledge those groups contributed relatively high to the overall floral disparity (see Lopez-Martinez et al 2024), why? -The comparison between pollen disparity and pollination mode was particularly interesting. The authors obtained the data of pollination mode from Stephens et al.; however, to my knowledge, the sampling might be substantially different. Stephens et al. included about 1200 extant taxa, with pollination mode mostly scored at species level, which contrasts with the sampling presented in this study. The authors should clarify these differences and explain how they account for the variation on pollination type within a Genera (e.g., Aquilegia shows vertebrate and insect pollination or even exhibit a mixed pollination strategies). Minor comments: The measure of disparity based on the sum of variances using the NMDS and PCoA ordination can be problematic when using discrete morphological characters. I think it is more accurate to measure disparity based on the distance matrix (please see Gerber, 2019. Use and misuse of discrete character data for morphospace and disparity analyses. Palaeontology 62: 305-319).

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This is a fascinating and well-written paper. It provides a much-needed analysis of
the phylogenetic pattern of pollen morphology and produces insights into the timing
of angiosperm diversification.
>>> Thank you for your thorough review and positive insights. We appreciate all
the comments and have addressed all of them below.
My expertise is in palynology and less so in phylogenetic methods, so my
comments focus more on the morphological analysis than the phylogenetic work.
That said, however, my main concern with the paper is the angiosperm phylogeny
used in the study. The authors produce their own from published sequence data
instead of relying on recently published phylogenies (e.g., Zuntini et al 2024). I do
not believe that this will affect the interpretations or conclusions of the paper, given
the broad patterns that this paper focuses on, but the authors should be aware that
there will be a mismatch between the superorder clades that they discuss (Fabids,
Malvids, Superasterids, Superrosids) and more recent delimitations. Given the
speed at which genomic data is now being accumulated, and the potential for future
reorganization of the angiosperm phylogeny, it would be helpful if the authors
included a spreadsheet of the genera and orders they include within their larger
named groups to help with transparency and interpretability of their analysis.
>>> Thank you for your suggestion. We have listed the orders and major clade
affiliations of all sampled angiosperm genera included in our study in Supplemental
Data 1, following both APG IV (2016) and Zuntini et al. (2024). We have also clearly
stated this in the Methods section and highlight the differences between the two
classification systems, see lines 555-559.
Above the ordinal level, naming conventions within the APG system have remained
fluid and largely informal. APG III (2009) recognized the need for names
corresponding to the major clades of angiosperms, given that the entire clade is
treated as a single subclass. In response, Chase and Reveal (2009) proposed a
classification with 18 superorders. However, APG IV did not adopt this system and
instead introduced the new informal terms Superasterids and Superrosids to assist
communication and comprehension.
In our study, although the phylogenetic tree is based on both plastid and nuclear
genes, the recovered ordinal-level relationships are largely consistent with those
recognized by APG IV. Therefore, we adopted the informal clade names endorsed
by the APG system. These names have become widely accepted within the
botanical community and serve a practical purpose in facilitating communication
across disciplines.
Zuntini et al. (2024) represents a major update to our understanding of angiosperm
relationships. Their study recovered 58 of the 64 currently accepted orders and
406 of the 416 families as monophyletic and confirmed 85% of the inter-family
relationships reported in our Plastid Phylogenomic Angiosperm II (PPA II) project
(Li et al., 2021).
Notably, Zuntini et al. (2024) proposed a recircumscription of fabids and malvids,
where the new fabid clade (Cucurbitales, Fabales, Fagales, and Rosales)
corresponds to what was previously defined as the nitrogen-fixing clade, while the
former COM clade (Celastrales–Oxalidales–Malpighiales) is now placed within
malvids. It is worth noting that APG IV had already acknowledged potential
cytonuclear discordance within the COM clade based on earlier nuclear and
mitochondrial data, and this uncertainty was explicitly marked in their ordinal-level
chronograms.
Zuntini et al. (2024) also introduced adjustments to the placements of several
orders, particularly those previously unassigned to the four major monophyletic
clades of core eudicots (campanulids, lamiids, fabids, and malvids), such as
Caryophyllales, Santalales, Dilleniales, Gunnerales, Bruniales, and Icacinales. At
the same time, we note that definitions and interrelationships among major
angiosperm groups—especially within the core eudicots—still vary across different
versions of the Kew Tree of Life Explorer (https://treeoflife.kew.org/tree-of-life)
associated with the Zuntini et al. (2024) phylogeny.
We are confident that through continued international collaboration and
consensus-building—as reflected in the APG framework—these discrepancies will
gradually be resolved, and a stable and broadly accepted classification will emerge.
Refs cited in this Reply:
APG IV. An update of the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group classification for the
orders and families of flowering plants: APG IV. Bot J Linn Soc 181, 1-20 (2016).
Chase M. W., Reveal J. L. A phylogenetic classification of the land plants to
accompany APG III. Bot J Linn Soc 161, 122-127 (2009).
Li H.-T., et al. Plastid phylogenomic insights into relationships of all flowering plant
families. BMC Biol 19, 232 (2021).
Zuntini A. R., et al. Phylogenomics and the rise of the angiosperms. Nature 629,
843-850 (2024).
I would also strongly encourage the authors to publish the list of genera in their
analysis and their character scores as a second spreadsheet. This again would
improve the transparency and interpretability of their analysis and encourage
others to build on their work.

characterize pollen grains across a large set of species. On the author hand the

evolutionary history of these characters. By combining these two datasets and
using comparative methods, they make a case for pulsed evolution of pollen. I think

the extensive series of papers on the “Evolution of Angiosperm Pollen”.
>>> We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive and encouraging feedback.
A few questions I have are the following: Why a genus level pollen dataset?
Are all the genera included monophyletic? Do the authors have any concern that
if a genus in the dataset is not monophyletic their results would change? What
happens when a genus is polymorphic for a trait? How does it get scored? What
effect does it have to calculate disparity through time when the terminals in the tree
are genera and not species?
>>> We thank the reviewer for these thoughtful and important questions regarding
our use of a genus-level pollen dataset. Below we respond to each point in turn:
(1) Why use genera as terminal units?
We chose the genus level for several reasons. First, genus-level sampling is widely
used in macroevolutionary studies as a way to reduce species-level sampling
biases while still capturing meaningful proxies for ecological and morphological
diversity (Jablonski 2017). Notably, Linnaean genera continue to be treated as
biologically meaningful units, and the evolutionary reality of both species and
genera has been extensively discussed (e.g., Barraclough and Humphreys, 2015).
Among higher taxa, genera often exhibit the highest degree of evolutionary
coherence or “shared fate”, reflected in shared evolutionary trajectories and
predictable morphological patterns among constituent species.
Second, evolutionary signals tend to vary by taxonomic rank: higher-level clades
often represent the emergence of new body plans, while lower-level clades capture
the dynamics of species formation and turnover (Valentine 2004; Wagner 2014;
Jablonski 2017). Since our focus is on large-scale evolutionary patterns in pollen
morphology, intra-generic evolutionary history lies beyond the scope of this study.
Third, the genus level has long been the primary taxonomic unit in palynology, both
for extant and fossil taxa, largely because of the morphological homogeneity of
pollen among species within genera. Pollen morphology is traditionally described
at the genus level, resulting in a wealth of comparative data at that rank. Although
species-level datasets would be ideal, the current state of taxonomic and
8
morphological coverage makes genus-level sampling both more feasible and more
comprehensive.
(2) Are all included genera monophyletic, and what is the effect of using genera
rather than species as terminals?
This is closely related to the previous point. Although genera are not perfect units,
they typically correspond well to genealogical groups and can effectively serve as
proxies for low-level clades of closely related species (Jablonski 2017). In our study,
we carefully checked the taxonomic status of each genus using global databases
such as the Catalogue of Life (COL) and Plants of the World Online (POWO).
When building the phylogeny, we excluded taxa with uncertain placements to
ensure the monophyly of accepted genera, families, and orders.
Most currently accepted angiosperm genera are now well circumscribed and are
generally supported as monophyletic by available molecular data, even in large-
scale supermatrix analyses with incomplete sampling (e.g., Zanne et al. 2014;
Smith et al. 2018). In addition, our sampling strategy emphasized broad
phylogenetic representativeness, including all major angiosperm orders and most
major intrafamilial clades, ensuring that deeper branching events leading to extant
lineages were well captured.
To evaluate the stability of our disparity-through-time analyses, we also performed
100 replicate analyses based on random subsampling of 1000 genera from our
dataset. These analyses consistently recovered similar temporal patterns,
including pulses of morphological disparity, indicating that our key results are
robust to variation in taxon sampling and are unlikely to be artifacts of genus-level
non-monophyly.
(3) How is polymorphism within genera handled in character scoring?
To represent known within-genus variation, we adopted a polymorphic coding
strategy that retains all observed states without modification (e.g., scoring ‘0&1&2’).
This remains one of the most commonly used methods for scoring polymorphisms
in discrete characters (Wortley et al. 2015; Watanabe 2016), especially when
character state frequencies are not well known. While frequency-based coding
may in principle offer greater resolution, it is infeasible for our dataset due to the
limited availability of species-level pollen data for many genera. Subsequent
analysis workflow for calculating pairwise distances (MORD distance metric) can
handle polymorphisms.
Alternative approaches such as “democratic coding” (scoring only the most
common state) have been used in some of our prior work, but we chose not to
apply this here because it introduces subjective assumptions (e.g., equating
frequency with ancestral state). Given current data limitations, we believe that
retaining observed polymorphisms is a more transparent and biologically honest
approach.
Overall, our focus on discrete, basic traits of pollen morphology, coupled with a
broad macroevolutionary scope targeting deep divergences in angiosperm history,
supports the use of genus-level units and polymorphic coding. We have further
9
clarified our rationale for this approach in the Methods (lines 537-551, 580-595)
and Supplementary Methods sections.

>>> We appreciate the reviewer’s careful attention to our character definitions,
and we acknowledge that additional clarification is warranted. We have now added
a more detailed explanation to the Supplementary Methods, and provide a
summary here:
Wortley et al. (2015), the comprehensive overview of the "Evolution of Angiosperm
Pollen" series, outlines our character selection and coding approach. The study
builds upon classic palynological literature and breaks down complex or composite
terms into their most fundamental components.
Following Walker and Doyle (1975), angiosperm pollen shape can be broadly
categorized as either nonfixiform (without a definite shape, e.g., filiform grains) or
fixiform (with a definite shape). The latter can be further divided into two major
shape classes: boat-shaped and globose. Wortley et al. (2015) adopted this
framework. However, “basic shape” alone is insufficient to describe pollen
morphology comprehensively. It has thus become standard to describe shape
10
using two additional traits—equatorial and polar views. In equatorial view, grains
are categorized by shape class, defined by the ratio of the polar to equatorial axes
(P/E). In polar view, outlines are described using more specific terms such as
circular, elliptic, polygonal, or lobate. Together, these three descriptors—basic
shape, shape class, and outline in polar view—offer a composite description of the
3D shape of pollen grains. It is important to note that filiform pollen represents a
special case for which most shape descriptors become inapplicable. For such
grains, only basic shape is scored, and equatorial or polar outlines are coded as
“not applicable”.
In practice, pollen shape is often influenced by the harmomegathic effect (also
known as the Wodehouse effect), especially in herbarium or fossil material
(Halbritter and Hesse, 2004). This phenomenon can cause pollen grains to
collapse in varied and unpredictable ways, significantly altering their apparent
morphology. In our dataset, seven characters describe grain shape (characters 1–
7), including basic shape, outline in polar view, and size, all of which can be
affected to some degree by harmomegathy.
Because our study integrates data from diverse sources—each capturing pollen
grains at different hydration states—we adopted a harmonized coding strategy. For
the basic shape character, we follow the conceptual distinction between
nonfixiform and fixiform pollen. For boat-shaped grains, we note that although Punt
et al. (2007) did not define this state, Halbritter et al. (2018) described it as “a
characteristic shape of sulcate pollen grains in dry condition as a consequence of
harmomegathy.” While this term can be useful in paleopalynology, particularly for
identifying monosulcate grains under light microscopy, we generally excluded it
from disparity analyses due to its high plasticity. Recent studies of pollen
mechanics and geometry have shown that transitions from globose to boat-shaped
forms under desiccation are strongly influenced by aperture architecture (Katifori
et al. 2010; Božič et al. 2019).
The shape class character, likewise influenced by hydration state, is typically
inapplicable to boat-shaped grains. Wortley et al. (2015) found this trait to be highly
homoplastic and relatively uninformative for phylogenetic inference. In our initial
scoring, this character was missing in over 70% of genera—far exceeding our 25%
threshold for reliable inclusion. For these reasons, we excluded shape class from
all disparity and morphospace analyses.
We hope this additional clarification addresses the reviewer’s concern, and we
have updated the Supplementary Methods to reflect this explanation in full.

Major comment
is that the estimation of pollen variation through time is based solely on extant
taxa. I find no adequate justification for completely disregarding the valuable
knowledge that has been compiled over decades by the paleobotanical
community on the fossil pollen record. In my view, the fossil pollen record
represents the only direct source of information for assessing morphological
disparity in the deep past, and its analysis and quantification are essential for a
comprehensive understanding of evolutionary patterns over time. More reliable
macroevolutionary inferences require the inclusion of fossil taxa, as there are
many examples in which the fossil record contain much more information about
past evolutionary patterns than phylogenies, for example preserving unique
character combinations that have not seen in living species and consequently
cannot be reconstructed in ancestral state reconstructions. Incorporating such
fossil data could significantly change the observed patterns of disparity through
time.
The authors indicate that earlier studies fossil pollen (e.g., Lupia, 1999; Doyle
1977) “were constrained by a limited understanding of evolutionary
relationships among groups and were restricted in geographical and temporal
extent”. I agree with this assessment; however, I believe that significant
progress has been made in recent decades to improve our understanding of
the fossil pollen record. For example, new species have been described (many
with a great detail) and new localities have been sampled greatly expanding
the temporal and geographical coverage of available data. I am not saying that
the fossil record is perfect, fossil data are subject to several biases, but also
inferring these patterns using the phylogenies of extant taxa is not accurate.
This is my main concern; the approach considered in this study, while
methodologically sound with its scope, may fall short of what is expected for a
Nature Communications paper, especially compared to a recent article on a
similar topic (Clark et al. 2023 Nat Plants), which integrated fossil and extant
data to assess morphological disparity. One potential solution for this pitfall is
that the authors should be explicit about the estimations based only on extant
taxa, for example in the title or in the abstract.

findings, you indicate that rates of pollen evolution remained stable during the
mid-Cretaceous and Paleogene. However, what does the pollen fossil record
reveal about the Late Cretaceous? How did morphological diversification
proceed during this interval? Was it similarly stable and low, or were there
notable shifts in morphology? Additionally, which new morphological characters
first appeared during this period? A discussion of these aspects would
significantly enrich the interpretation of your results within a broader
evolutionary and paleobotanical context.
The main strength of this paper, in my view, is that the authors, given their taxon
sampling, are able to offer a comprehensive comparison of disparity variation
15
among extant angiosperm clades or lineages and provide a further discussion
on this variation.
>>> We fully agree that the fossil pollen record offers invaluable insights into past
morphological disparity and long-term evolutionary dynamics, and acknowledge
that significant progress has been made in recent decades in paleopalynology. We
have added additional text to the discussion (section ‘Two Main Pulses in
Angiosperm Pollen Disparity’) that links our findings, and particularly the increases
in disparity during the mid-Cretaceous and Paleogene, to the fossil pollen record.
We have also updated the title and added explicit statements in both the Abstract
and Discussion noting that our analyses are based solely on extant taxa.
Integrating the morphological diversity of both extant and fossil pollen across the
whole angiosperms remains an extraordinarily challenging task. As noted in the
introduction to the paper, our aim in this study was to work in an explicit
phylogenetic context to allow us to analyse both disparity through time and rates
of morphological evolution. The plant fossil record, however, is mostly comprised
of allochthonous and fragmentary remains (Cleal et al. 2021) that are challenging
to meaningfully include in phylogenetic analyses. Even rigorously evaluating the
taxonomic affinities (e.g., to orders or families) of early angiosperm pollen types
remains challenging, with many pre-Neogene palynotaxa having uncertain
botanical affiliations (Cleal et al. 2021; Friis et al. 2024). Consequently, large-scale
syntheses of the angiosperm fossil record often omit pollen from their datasets
(e.g., Silvestro et al. 2021) —a marked contrast with the rich, regionally detailed
palynostratigraphic studies.
Incorporating large pollen fossil datasets—collected across widely varying
geographical and temporal scales—into an extant-focused phylogenetic
framework without introducing bias is therefore beyond the scope of this study,
although this is an important direction for future work.
We also note that the recent study by Clark et al. (2023), which incorporated fossil
data to analyze disparity across the entire plant kingdom, relied on a limited subset
of assignable fossils and did not report any substantial changes in the overall
macroevolutionary patterns resulting from their inclusion. Their broader
phylogenetic scope have allowed more reliable assignment of plant macrofossil to
higher-level clades (e.g., class).
Ultimately, paleontologists and neontologists investigate the same tree of life, and
a comprehensive understanding of macroevolution must be informed by both
phylogenetic inference from living lineages and direct evidence from the fossil
record.
Refs cited in this Reply:
Clark J. W., et al. Evolution of phenotypic disparity in the plant kingdom. Nature
Plants 9, 1618-1626 (2023).
Cleal C., et al. Palaeobotanical experiences of plant diversity in deep time. 1: How
well can we identify past plant diversity in the fossil record? Palaeogeogr,
Friis E. M., Crane P. R., Pedersen K. R. The Cretaceous diversification of
angiosperms: perspectives from mesofossils. Geological Society, London, Special
Publications 544, 393-432 (2024).
Silvestro D., et al. Fossil data support a pre-Cretaceous origin of flowering plants.
Nature Ecology & Evolution 5, 449-457 (2021).
For example:
-why some extant clades appeared more restricted in the space than others? I
see that the authors explained this topic in the section of “extant angiosperm
pollen morphospace”, however, it would be interesting to know, for example:
-the extensive morphospace occupation by fabids aligns with patterns observed
in studies of floral or leaf morphospaces?
>>> Within eudicots, López-Martínez et al. (2024) showed that floral disparity in
fabids, the other superrosids grade, and the other superasterids grade was
comparable, though all were lower than in the other eudicots grade. In contrast,
our results on pollen disparity indicate that fabids exhibit the second highest
disparity level, only after the other superasterids grade. This highlights that
different morphological systems (floral vs. pollen traits) can reveal distinct aspects
of morphological diversification.
To address the reviewers’ comments regarding morphospace comparisons, we
have moved the section “Extant Angiosperm Pollen Morphospace” to the beginning
of the Discussion and expanded its content to provide a more comprehensive
explanation of pollen morphospace structure, see lines 287-321.
Refs cited in this Reply:
López-Martínez A. M., Magallón S., von Balthazar M., Schönenberger J., Sauquet
H., Chartier M. Angiosperm flowers reached their highest morphological diversity
early in their evolutionary history. New Phytol 241, 1348-1360 (2024).
-Why do monocots exhibit the highest morphological disparity despite not
occupying the largest areas of the morphospace?
>>> Monocots show the highest values in three indices (SOV, MPD, MDC), which
reflect internal spread, while not occupying the largest morphospace area (as
measured by SOR), which reflects the overall extent of trait combinations. This
suggests that monocot pollen forms are highly dispersed but within a more
restricted region of the morphospace.
-The ANA grade, Chloranthales, and the other superasterids groups have the
lowest contributions to the overall disparity, however, to my knowledge those
groups contributed relatively high to the overall floral disparity (see Lopez-
Martinez et al 2024), why?
>>> For example, the “other superasterids” group shows the highest disparity level
among eudicots but contributes little to the overall disparity of eudicots. As Foote
(1993) noted, a subgroup’s disparity and its contribution to total disparity are not
always correlated. Groups that lie at the periphery of morphospace and span
distinct regions tend to increase overall disparity more. In contrast, the other
superasterids, though internally diverse, occupy a region already densely filled by
other eudicots, resulting in limited impact on the total morphospace expansion.
As for the contrast with López-Martínez et al. (2024), which focused on floral
disparity, we agree that this is an interesting result. The difference likely reflects
the use of different morphologic systems—pollen versus floral traits—which are
shaped by different developmental and evolutionary constraints. Disparity patterns
can vary depending on the morphological domain under study, and such variation
is to be expected. We have contrasted our pollen disparity results with the floral
analysis of López-Martínez et al. (2024) on lines 298-309.
Refs cited in this Reply:
López-Martínez A. M., Magallón S., von Balthazar M., Schönenberger J., Sauquet
H., Chartier M. Angiosperm flowers reached their highest morphological diversity
early in their evolutionary history. New Phytol 241, 1348-1360 (2024).
Foote M. (1993) Contributions of individual taxa to overall morphological disparity.
Paleobiology 19, 403-419.
-The comparison between pollen disparity and pollination mode was particularly
interesting. The authors obtained the data of pollination mode from Stephens
et al.; however, to my knowledge, the sampling might be substantially different.
Stephens et al. included about 1200 extant taxa, with pollination mode mostly
scored at species level, which contrasts with the sampling presented in this
study. The authors should clarify these differences and explain how they
account for the variation on pollination type within a Genera (e.g., Aquilegia
shows vertebrate and insect pollination or even exhibit a mixed pollination
strategies).
>>> We clarified this in the Methods that Stephens et al. (2023) compiled
pollination mode data primarily at the species level. In fact, we initially assembled
genus-level pollination mode annotations for all sampled taxa using the TRY and
BIEN databases, supplemented with information from related literatures. Our
preliminary analyses based on this dataset yielded results that were highly
consistent with those derived from Stephens et al. (2023). Given the challenges
and subjectivity involved in scoring pollination mode and the overall concordance
of results, we ultimately adopted the dataset from Stephens et al. (2023) for clarity
and consistency.
Regarding the concern about within-genus variation in pollination mode, we note
18
that such genera are excluded from the morphospace analysis, as stated in the
Methods (lines 687-690).
Refs cited in this Reply:
Stephens R. E., Gallagher R. V., Dun L., Cornwell W., Sauquet H. Insect pollination
for most of angiosperm evolutionary history. New Phytol 240, 880-891 (2023).
Minor comments:
The measure of disparity based on the sum of variances using the NMDS and
PCoA ordination can be problematic when using discrete morphological
characters. I think it is more accurate to measure disparity based on the
distance matrix (please see Gerber, 2019. Use and misuse of discrete
character data for morphospace and disparity analyses. Palaeontology 62: 305-
319).
>>> We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the use of ordinated spaces
for disparity metrics.
Among the four size-related disparity indices we used, only Mean Pairwise
Distance (MPD) can be directly calculated from the raw distance matrix, and it is
also one of the recommended metrics in Gerber (2019).
To evaluate the reliability of ordination-based estimates, we compared MPD values
derived from the raw distance matrix (i.e., without ordination) and from ordinated
coordinates (post-ordination). NMDS-derived MPD values were highly correlated
with the raw values (Pearson’s r = 0.957, p < 0.001), indicating minimal distortion
of the relative structure of morphological distances (see Supplementary Fig. 2). In
contrast, PCoA-based MPD showed a relatively weaker correlation (r = 0.737, p =
0.006), reflecting greater information loss during dimensionality reduction.
These results support the reliability of our NMDS-based estimates, which we
primarily used. Given this strong concordance, we are confident that our approach
does not bias the results or affect the interpretation of disparity patterns.
We have further added sentences in the Methods and Result sections (lines 175-
179, 635-638).
Refs cited in this Reply:
Gerber S. Use and misuse of discrete character data for morphospace and
disparity analyses. Palaeontology 62, 305-319 (2019).
Sincerely Yours,
De-Zhu Li PhD FLS OBE FRSE
Professor of Botany
19

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: Major comment: I appreciate that my comments have been taken into account in this revised version of the manuscript. I believe that the efforts made by the authors to address the suggestions have contributed to improve the quality of this investigation. I appreciate how the authors presented the results and discussion in this new version. However, I would like to see a further discussion on the evolution of the pollen form. For example, which phenotypes are the most common ones? To what extent might these patterns reflect phylogenetic constraints versus evolutionary convergence? Which characters might be responsible for the saturation of certain areas of the morphospace? A particularly relevant study by Luke Mander (see citation below) explores this issue using a “raw” morphospace approach, although it focuses exclusively on pollen from tropical angiosperm species. For example, Mander demonstrates how monocots and eudicots occupy different regions of the morphospace and highlights associations between various discrete characters. He found that pollen grains observed in nature occupy considerable amount of the raw morphospace (which in a certain way study the evolution of forms within those that are possible). In your case, you found a contrast pattern of occupation. Could this be a consequence of not constraining the theoretical morphospace? Are there combinations included in your theoretical morphospace that may in fact be biologically impossible? I believe this work provides an interesting point of comparison for your study and should be considered, especially since it has not yet been cited. Mander Luke. 2016. A combinatorial approach to angiosperm pollen morphology. Proc. R. Soc. B.28320162033. http://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2016.2033 Minor comments: L109-110: “and the prevalent issue of microfossil identification bias complicates macroevolutionary modeling efforts”. For example, in L211 you use “other superasterids” and here you use “other superasterid grade” L233 Could you provide the value of character state changes per my? Just for comparison with the previous sentence. L304. Avoid “basally”-branching L544. Mentioning fossils here is not relevant for your study. L648 The authors state that they were inspired by the simulations of Deline et al. to construct the theoretical morphospace. However, the procedure they describe for generating the theoretical combinations closely resembles the approach presented by López Martínez et al. Therefore, I suggest that this paper should at least be cited in the Methods section to recognize this precedent. L659-660: Same approach as Lopez Martinez et al. This paper should be cited. L688. biotic types, and wind, water, insect, and vertebrate types -> biotic types, and wind, water, insect, and vertebrate types? L 690. genera. It would be good if the authors could confirm that that is the case for the

pollen form. For example, which phenotypes are the most common ones? To what

>>> We agree that interpreting the high-dimensional morphospace constructed
from discrete coding is a major challenge. To aid interpretation beyond overall
pollen disparity, we also analyzed three subsets of traits (shape, aperture, and

substantially expanded analyses that might go beyond the scope and central focus

phylogenetic constraints and evolutionary convergence shape morphospace
occupation. In response to your suggestion, we have incorporated additional
analyses of morphological convergence, which yielded intriguing results.

analyses, these results provide a more refined perspective on how extant
angiosperm pollen occupies morphospace.

Results, and Discussion (see Results, lines 183–190, 225–244; Discussion, lines
336–359; Methods, lines 629–632, 651–663). We believe that these revisions

investigations into the evolution of pollen form.

associations between various discrete characters. He found that pollen grains
observed in nature occupy considerable amount of the raw morphospace (which

not constraining the theoretical morphospace? Are there combinations included in
your theoretical morphospace that may in fact be biologically impossible? I believe
this work provides an interesting point of comparison for your study and should be

Mander Luke. 2016. A combinatorial approach to angiosperm pollen morphology.
Proc. R. Soc. B.28320162033. http://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2016.2033
>>> Thank you for raising this important point. In our analyses, we explicitly
restricted inapplicable or biologically impossible trait combinations. However, we
realized that in our initial phrasing we mistakenly described our results as
“occupying an area,” which implied the use of the sum of ranges (SOR), whereas
our calculations were actually based on the sum of variances (SOV). In our results,
the empirical pollen morphospace occupies 89.6% of the theoretical morphospace
4
in terms of SOR, but only 49% in terms of SOV. This contrast indicates that while
the boundaries of pollen morphospace are extensively explored, the realized
distribution is highly concentrated. Notably, in Mander (2016), pollen grains
observed in nature were found to occupy a considerable portion of the raw
morphospace. Views through the lens of our SOR results, extant angiosperms
have explored the boundaries of morphospace to a substantial degree. It should
be noted, however, that both SOR and SOV differ methodologically from the raw
morphospace approach of Mander (2016), with SOR being comparatively more
sensitive to outliers.
Furthermore, in subsequent analyses of phylogenetic signal and
morphological convergence, our results reveal a complex interplay between
phylogenetic constraints and convergence. Interestingly, despite differences in
methodological frameworks and coding strategies, our findings are broadly in line
with those of Mander (2016), both in terms of morphospace occupation and
convergent evolution. While our approach is based on distance matrices and
ordination, Mander’s combinatorial “raw morphospace” framework provides a more
direct perspective on the potential versus realized spectrum of pollen forms. We
now explicitly cite and discuss Mander (2016). We also note his more recent work
on floral morphology (Mander et al. 2025), which highlights the broader utility of
this combinatorial approach.

accordingly, and corrected the earlier misstatement regarding SOR versus SOV
(see lines 183–190, 336–359).

Mander L., Julier A. C. M., Jaramillo C. The architecture of floral diversity: a

highlight the phylogenetic relationships among the five major mesangiosperm
clades.

superasterids/eudicots/monocots/superrosids”.

>>> We replaced “basally-branching” with “early-diverging”.
L544. Mentioning fossils here is not relevant for your study.
>>> Revised. We have removed the phrase “especially in fossil and herbarium
material”.
L648 The authors state that they were inspired by the simulations of Deline et al.
to construct the theoretical morphospace. However, the procedure they describe
for generating the theoretical combinations closely resembles the approach
presented by López Martínez et al. In fact, the figures included in this manuscript
are quite similar to those shown in López Martínez et al. Therefore, I suggest that
this paper should at least be cited in the Methods section to recognize this
precedent.
>>> We had previously noted the work of López-Martínez et al. (2024) on
theoretical morphospace but had not fully understood their methodology. After
carefully re-examining their description, we now recognize that our procedure for
generating theoretical combinations is broadly similar to theirs. We have therefore

López-Martínez A. M., Magallón S., von Balthazar M., Schönenberger J., Sauquet
H., Chartier M. Angiosperm flowers reached their highest morphological diversity
early in their evolutionary history. New Phytol 241, 1348-1360 (2024).
L659-660: Same approach as Lopez Martinez et al. This paper should be cited.
6
>>> See above.

wind, water, insect, and vertebrate types?
>>> Revised.
L 690. For me it is not entirely clear how the authors deal with polymorphic data.
As far as I know, Stephens et al. used polymorphism to conduct their ASR.
They only treated missing data in correlation analyses between high latitude and wind
pollination.
>>> In our correlation analyses we did not perform ancestral state reconstructions;
all data were restricted to extant taxa. Genera with polymorphic states were
excluded both from the Pearson correlation tests and from the comparisons of
morphospace occupation across different pollination modes (Extended Data Figs.
9–10). We have clarified this point in the Methods section and also specified the
exact number of genera included in the pollination-related analyses (see lines 686–
698).
Refs cited in this Reply:
Stephens R. E., Gallagher R. V., Dun L., Cornwell W., Sauquet H. Insect pollination
for most of angiosperm evolutionary history. New Phytol 240, 880-891 (2023).
Figure 4. Avoid using BASAL in the figures.
>>> Revised.

Professor of Botany

### Reviewer 1

This is a fascinating and well-written paper. It provides a much-needed analysis of the phylogenetic pattern of pollen morphology and produces insights into the timing of angiosperm diversification. My expertise is in palynology and less so in phylogenetic methods, so my comments focus more on the morphological analysis than the phylogenetic work. That said, however, my main concern with the paper is the angiosperm phylogeny used in the study. The authors produce their own from published sequence data instead of relying on recently published phylogenies (e.g., Zuntini et al 2024). I do not believe that this will affect the interpretations or conclusions of the paper, given the broad patterns that this paper focuses on, but the authors should be aware that there will be a mismatch between the superorder clades that they discuss (Fabids, Malvids, Superasterids, Superrosids) and more recent delimitations. Given the speed at which genomic data is now being accumulated, and the potential for future reorganization of the angiosperm phylogeny, it would be helpful if the authors included a spreadsheet of the genera and orders they include within their larger named groups to help with transparency and interpretability of their analysis. I would also strongly encourage the authors to publish the list of genera in their analysis and their character scores as a second spreadsheet. This again would improve the transparency and interpretability of their analysis and encourage others to build on their work. Section-by-section points below: Abstract • “Endowed” is an odd word choice. Maybe simply “composed”? Introduction • Page 3, line 3: “synapomorphy OF equatorially tricolpate pollen” • “the processes of angiosperm pollen diversification”: This paper is more about pattern than process. Suggest that you emphasize the importance of documenting pattern to infer process. • “This gap hinders, and may even distort, our understanding of angiosperm radiation, particularly regarding deep evolutionary processes”: I agree with the sentiment, but it would be better if the authors made a more explicit statement of how this is a result of the previous sentence. Results • p 4: “a discrete-coded matrix”: Should note that 20 characters were coded, and the larger groupings (aperture, exine, shape) should be introduced and described/defined. Otherwise, the meaning of the shorthand terms used in the results (aperture, exine, shape) are hard to understand. • p 4: “The topology is congruent with recent phylogenetic frameworks 48-50”: Note that Zuntini et al 2024 does NOT have the same topology as previous phylogenies (e.g., APG IV) • p 5, paragraph 1: “plastome-based PPA tree”: Should include “the” before the word “plastome”. Also need to define what this is, particularly the acronym PPA. • p 5, paragraph 1: “a temporal pattern irreconcilable with current paleobotanical evidence”: It is not clear whether you are saying your results are irreconcilable or whether old tree scenarios are. Based on Coiro et al 2019 review of the Triassic fossil evidence, I would say that phylogenies that place the ancestral angiosperm node very early (Triassic or before) conflict most with the paleo record. • p 5, paragraph 2: “In our ordination analysis, we opted for Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS) to process the pollen data”: process is not the correct word. Interpret? Analyze? • p 5: Pollen morphospace occupation (and elsewhere): all palynological terms should be defined when first introduced. When mentioning a trait (e.g., polarity), mention which larger grouping it belongs to (aperture, exine, shape). • p 5, last paragraph: “Compared to the theoretical morphospace, the empirical morphospace occupies approximately 43% of the area on the left side”: Language here is too casual and imprecise. Right vs left is arbitrary in a multivariate analysis. What is important is that only a portion of the theoretical morphospace is occupied. Instead of left and right, describe the axis by the traits with which it most strongly covaries, positively and negatively. • p 6, paragraph 1: “the highest levels”: What does this mean? • p 6, paragraph 1: “overall pollen disparity”: Is this within-clade or between clades? • p 7, paragraph 1: “overlap between the two lists”: What two lists? If this is a reference to Table S5, include the reference and explain the difference between the two sets of rankings. Discussion • p 9, paragraph 2: “These differences emphasize that varying scales and subjects of observation can yield different evolutionary insights.”: Is the argument that early pollen evolution was constrained? The wording is a little vague. • p 9, paragraph 3: “In animal taxa, basally-branching groups often exhibit higher levels of disparity than their more derived counterparts 15,24,25, a pattern also observed in the morphospace of angiosperm flowers 41,56.” This is repetitive, as the same point is made in the previous paragraph. • p 10: Synchronous Evolution of Pollen and Leaves: This section is speculative and has a tenuous connection to the rest of the paper. How does tricolpate pollen relate to hot wet environments? Recommend removing this section. • p 11, last paragraph: “while the Malpighiales are associated with the development of neotropical rainforests”: Need a citation for this. Malpighiales is a large and diverse order, but it is Malvales that is the more important Neotropical clade. Conclusions • Appreciate the mention of extinct diversity! Methods • p 15, paragraph 3: “with further subdivisions for detailed analysis”: As noted at the start of the review, you should specify that you are following APG IV clade deliminations, not Zuntini et al 2024. It is important that you list the orders and genera within each larger named group in a supplemental spreadsheet. • p 16, paragraph 1: More detail on how the theoretical morphospace was calculated would be helpful. Presumably these are random permutations of the pollen characters in Table S2 (which should be referenced here). Supporting information • Supplementary Table 2: A third column is needed to indicate which larger grouping each trait falls under (aperture, shape, exine). Happy to clarify any of the above comments. Surangi Punyasena (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)

### Reviewer 2

Dear Authors and Editor, I have reviewed the paper entitled "Pulsed evolution shaped angiosperm pollen disparity". I think it is a good study addressing the evolution of a very important plant character. On the one hand the authors scored several pollen traits to characterize pollen grains across a large set of species. On the author hand the authors generated a time calibrated molecular phylogeny of plants to look at the evolutionary history of these characters. By combining these two datasets and using comparative methods, they make a case for pulsed evolution of pollen. I think the paper is clearly written and the authors build on their work on this topic, namely the extensive series of papers on the “Evolution of Angiosperm Pollen”. A few questions I have are the following: Why a genus level pollen dataset? Are all the genera included monophyletic? Do the authors have any concern that if a genus in the dataset is not monophyletic their results would change? What happens when a genus is polymorphic for a trait? How does it get scored? What effect does it have to calculate disparity through time when the terminals in the tree are genera and not species? When assigning shapes to the pollen, one character involves "Basic shape" whereas a second "Outline in polar view". It is not clear to me how these are independant. Also, the character states of the second one includes as state 0 "circular & elliptic". Where would an elliptic pollen grain in polar view fall in the "Basic shape" variable? Looking at studies that review these characteristics of pollen, Walker and Doyle (1975) for example divide pollen shape into two basic types: globose and boat shaped. Does this equal globose-like vs filiform? Hesse et al. (2009) divide shape into oblate, spheroidal and prolate. So perhaps a little explanation of how some of those variables were established would be useful. Why were the traditional shape scoreing not used? Several old and recent studies have used morphometrics, from traditional approaches employing length to width rations, to geometric morphometric techniques such as elliptic Fourier analyses. Is there a reason why the authors chose not to use a quantitative approach to measure pollen grain shape and instead stuck to a discrete and simplified way of scoring pollen? The size variable has very unequal bin sizes. How were those size classes determined? Maybe I missed it but the pollen characters used are subdivided into three subtypes but I don't think it is clear which characters are assigned to each subgroup. Maybe in Supplementary table 2 the subgroups could be pointed out. Supplemental Information Page 1, paragraph 2: change "Phylogenetic comparison methods" to "Phylogenetic comparative methods" I appreciate that all the scripts, data and code are made available.

### Reviewer 3

This study applies an impressive morphological dataset of pollen characters and a time-calibrated phylogeny to document morphospace occupation and changes in morphological diversity through time and across major angiosperm groups. I found this paper well-written and interesting to read. There are several points that I would like to highlight: 1) the taxon sampling for extant species is exceptionally good and the overall amount of missing data is low, an outcome that clearly reflects considerable effort by the authors; 2) I have no specific criticisms regarding the methods, as the authors employed and compared different ordination methods (NMDS and PCoA) as well as various and disparity indices (SOR, SOV, MPD, MDC). In my opinion, this is an interesting paper as allow us comparative analysis of morphological variation in other angiosperms organs, such as flowers, leaves, and wood providing a more comprehensive understanding of the evolutionary radiation of angiosperms. Major comment The lack of fossil data. Luo et al. are clearly aware of the limitation of this study is that the estimation of pollen variation through time is based solely on extant taxa. I find no adequate justification for completely disregarding the valuable knowledge that has been compiled over decades by the paleobotanical community on the fossil pollen record. In my view, the fossil pollen record represents the only direct source of information for assessing morphological disparity in the deep past, and its analysis and quantification are essential for a comprehensive understanding of evolutionary patterns over time. More reliable macroevolutionary inferences require the inclusion of fossil taxa, as there are many examples in which the fossil record contain much more information about past evolutionary patterns than phylogenies, for example preserving unique character combinations that have not seen in living species and consequently cannot be reconstructed in ancestral state reconstructions. Incorporating such fossil data could significantly change the observed patterns of disparity through time. The authors indicate that earlier studies fossil pollen (e.g., Lupia, 1999; Doyle 1977) “were constrained by a limited understanding of evolutionary relationships among groups and were restricted in geographical and temporal extent”. I agree with this assessment; however, I believe that significant progress has been made in recent decades to improve our understanding of the fossil pollen record. For example, new species have been described (many with a great detail) and new localities have been sampled greatly expanding the temporal and geographical coverage of available data. I am not saying that the fossil record is perfect, fossil data are subject to several biases, but also inferring these patterns using the phylogenies of extant taxa is not accurate. This is my main concern; the approach considered in this study, while methodologically sound with its scope, may fall short of what is expected for a Nature Communications paper, especially compared to a recent article on a similar topic (Clark et al. 2023 Nat Plants), which integrated fossil and extant data to assess morphological disparity. One potential solution for this pitfall is that the authors should be explicit about the estimations based only on extant taxa, for example in the title or in the abstract. I think that a section comparing the fossil record (not only the patterns observed by Lupia or Doyle) with your results is missing. For instance, based on your findings, you indicate that rates of pollen evolution remained stable during the mid-Cretaceous and Paleogene. However, what does the pollen fossil record reveal about the Late Cretaceous? How did morphological diversification proceed during this interval? Was it similarly stable and low, or were there notable shifts in morphology? Additionally, which new morphological characters first appeared during this period? A discussion of these aspects would significantly enrich the interpretation of your results within a broader evolutionary and paleobotanical context. The main strength of this paper, in my view, is that the authors, given their taxon sampling, are able to offer a comprehensive comparison of disparity variation among extant angiosperm clades or lineages and provide a further discussion on this variation. For example: -why some extant clades appeared more restricted in the space than others? I see that the authors explained this topic in the section of “extant angiosperm pollen morphospace”, however, it would be interesting to know, for example: -the extensive morphospace occupation by fabids aligns with patterns observed in studies of floral or leaf morphospaces? -Why do monocots exhibit the highest morphological disparity despite not occupying the largest areas of the morphospace? -The ANA grade, Chloranthales, and the other superasterids groups have the lowest contributions to the overall disparity, however, to my knowledge those groups contributed relatively high to the overall floral disparity (see Lopez-Martinez et al 2024), why? -The comparison between pollen disparity and pollination mode was particularly interesting. The authors obtained the data of pollination mode from Stephens et al.; however, to my knowledge, the sampling might be substantially different. Stephens et al. included about 1200 extant taxa, with pollination mode mostly scored at species level, which contrasts with the sampling presented in this study. The authors should clarify these differences and explain how they account for the variation on pollination type within a Genera (e.g., Aquilegia shows vertebrate and insect pollination or even exhibit a mixed pollination strategies). Minor comments: The measure of disparity based on the sum of variances using the NMDS and PCoA ordination can be problematic when using discrete morphological characters. I think it is more accurate to measure disparity based on the distance matrix (please see Gerber, 2019. Use and misuse of discrete character data for morphospace and disparity analyses. Palaeontology 62: 305-319).

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This is a fascinating and well-written paper. It provides a much-needed analysis of the phylogenetic pattern of pollen morphology and produces insights into the timing of angiosperm diversification. My expertise is in palynology and less so in phylogenetic methods, so my comments focus more on the morphological analysis than the phylogenetic work. That said, however, my main concern with the paper is the angiosperm phylogeny used in the study. The authors produce their own from published sequence data instead of relying on recently published phylogenies (e.g., Zuntini et al 2024). I do not believe that this will affect the interpretations or conclusions of the paper, given the broad patterns that this paper focuses on, but the authors should be aware that there will be a mismatch between the superorder clades that they discuss (Fabids, Malvids, Superasterids, Superrosids) and more recent delimitations. Given the speed at which genomic data is now being accumulated, and the potential for future reorganization of the angiosperm phylogeny, it would be helpful if the authors included a spreadsheet of the genera and orders they include within their larger named groups to help with transparency and interpretability of their analysis. I would also strongly encourage the authors to publish the list of genera in their analysis and their character scores as a second spreadsheet. This again would improve the transparency and interpretability of their analysis and encourage others to build on their work. Section-by-section points below: Abstract • “Endowed” is an odd word choice. Maybe simply “composed”? Introduction • Page 3, line 3: “synapomorphy OF equatorially tricolpate pollen” • “the processes of angiosperm pollen diversification”: This paper is more about pattern than process. Suggest that you emphasize the importance of documenting pattern to infer process. • “This gap hinders, and may even distort, our understanding of angiosperm radiation, particularly regarding deep evolutionary processes”: I agree with the sentiment, but it would be better if the authors made a more explicit statement of how this is a result of the previous sentence. Results • p 4: “a discrete-coded matrix”: Should note that 20 characters were coded, and the larger groupings (aperture, exine, shape) should be introduced and described/defined. Otherwise, the meaning of the shorthand terms used in the results (aperture, exine, shape) are hard to understand. • p 4: “The topology is congruent with recent phylogenetic frameworks 48-50”: Note that Zuntini et al 2024 does NOT have the same topology as previous phylogenies (e.g., APG IV) • p 5, paragraph 1: “plastome-based PPA tree”: Should include “the” before the word “plastome”. Also need to define what this is, particularly the acronym PPA. • p 5, paragraph 1: “a temporal pattern irreconcilable with current paleobotanical evidence”: It is not clear whether you are saying your results are irreconcilable or whether old tree scenarios are. Based on Coiro et al 2019 review of the Triassic fossil evidence, I would say that phylogenies that place the ancestral angiosperm node very early (Triassic or before) conflict most with the paleo record. • p 5, paragraph 2: “In our ordination analysis, we opted for Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS) to process the pollen data”: process is not the correct word. Interpret? Analyze? • p 5: Pollen morphospace occupation (and elsewhere): all palynological terms should be defined when first introduced. When mentioning a trait (e.g., polarity), mention which larger grouping it belongs to (aperture, exine, shape). • p 5, last paragraph: “Compared to the theoretical morphospace, the empirical morphospace occupies approximately 43% of the area on the left side”: Language here is too casual and imprecise. Right vs left is arbitrary in a multivariate analysis. What is important is that only a portion of the theoretical morphospace is occupied. Instead of left and right, describe the axis by the traits with which it most strongly covaries, positively and negatively. • p 6, paragraph 1: “the highest levels”: What does this mean? • p 6, paragraph 1: “overall pollen disparity”: Is this within-clade or between clades? • p 7, paragraph 1: “overlap between the two lists”: What two lists? If this is a reference to Table S5, include the reference and explain the difference between the two sets of rankings. Discussion • p 9, paragraph 2: “These differences emphasize that varying scales and subjects of observation can yield different evolutionary insights.”: Is the argument that early pollen evolution was constrained? The wording is a little vague. • p 9, paragraph 3: “In animal taxa, basally-branching groups often exhibit higher levels of disparity than their more derived counterparts 15,24,25, a pattern also observed in the morphospace of angiosperm flowers 41,56.” This is repetitive, as the same point is made in the previous paragraph. • p 10: Synchronous Evolution of Pollen and Leaves: This section is speculative and has a tenuous connection to the rest of the paper. How does tricolpate pollen relate to hot wet environments? Recommend removing this section. • p 11, last paragraph: “while the Malpighiales are associated with the development of neotropical rainforests”: Need a citation for this. Malpighiales is a large and diverse order, but it is Malvales that is the more important Neotropical clade. Conclusions • Appreciate the mention of extinct diversity! Methods • p 15, paragraph 3: “with further subdivisions for detailed analysis”: As noted at the start of the review, you should specify that you are following APG IV clade deliminations, not Zuntini et al 2024. It is important that you list the orders and genera within each larger named group in a supplemental spreadsheet. • p 16, paragraph 1: More detail on how the theoretical morphospace was calculated would be helpful. Presumably these are random permutations of the pollen characters in Table S2 (which should be referenced here). Supporting information • Supplementary Table 2: A third column is needed to indicate which larger grouping each trait falls under (aperture, shape, exine). Happy to clarify any of the above comments.
